strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: jointly modeling continuous trajectories and synchronous discrete events in multi-agent systems is a real gap, and the paper is, to my knowledge, the first to apply joint continuous-discrete diffusion to time-evolving multi-agent data (prior work covers static layouts, CAD, vision-language).

Technically sound formulation: the factorized forward process (Eq. 2-4), factorized reverse posterior with cross-modal conditioning through a shared denoiser (Eq. 5), and decomposed variational objective (Eq. 8) are correctly derived from DDPM and multinomial diffusion; the hybrid DDIM/multinomial sampling and misaligned beta-schedule alignment are sensible engineering contributions.

Comprehensive evaluation: three public sports datasets (NBA, NFL, Bundesliga), SOTA results on scene-level (SADE/SFDE) metrics in both future generation and imputation, comparison against many recent baselines (MoFlow, U2Diff, MART, Sports-Traj, etc.), human evaluation supporting the scene-level metrics, and extensive ablations (discrete steps, lambda, importance sampling, attention entropy interpretability).

Two new controllable generation tasks (weak-possessor-guidance and text-guidance) with the CrossGuid module, plus a new annotated benchmark (text descriptions for soccer/football) and a commitment to release data and code, which adds community value.
Honest limitations section addressing sparse-event (TPP) constraints and noisy NFL event attribution.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the core technique is a fairly direct combination of known components (Gaussian DDPM + multinomial diffusion as in DLT (Levi et al., 2023), CFG conditioning, cross-attention blocks). The contribution is primarily an application/domain novelty rather than a new generative principle.

Potential circularity in evaluation: possession events E are extracted from the same trajectories Y via a 1.5m heuristic, and guidance signals (GWPG, Gtext) are derived from these events; improvements in 'controllable accuracy' may partly reflect the model reproducing this heuristic rather than capturing true game semantics. No evaluation against independently annotated ground-truth events.

Gains over the closest baseline (U2Diff) are consistent but modest on several metrics, and the controllable-generation comparison is mostly against the authors' own ablated variant (w/o joint) rather than external controllable baselines; there is no baseline for the text-guidance task at all.

Some claims are stronger than evidence: 'joint modeling is crucial' rests largely on self-ablations, and the human study is small (15 participants, NBA only). Text-guidance is not evaluated on NBA, limiting completeness.

Dense-event assumption (one-hot possessor per timestep) is restrictive and the paper itself acknowledges it; the unified sports benchmark is only partially standardized across sports (different units, fps, agent counts), complicating cross-dataset claims.
Reproducibility depends on promised code/data release; LLM-generated captions introduce potential noise in the text-guidance benchmark that is not quantified.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: jointly modeling continuous trajectories and synchronous discrete events in multi-agent systems, with a sensible factorization of the forward process and a shared denoiser that conditions each modality on the other.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three sports datasets (NBA, NFL, BundesLiga), with completion (future + imputation) and two controllable generation tasks, plus a reasonable set of strong baselines (GroupNet, AutoBots, LED, MART, MoFlow, U2Diff, Sports-Traj, TranSPORTmer).

Useful ablations covering the discrete step schedule, loss weighting (lambda), importance sampling, and architecture components; the attention-entropy analysis in D.4 is a nice interpretability addition.

Honest discussion of limitations (dense-event assumption, heuristic actor assignment in NFL) and a human evaluation study supporting the claim that SADE/SFDE better reflect perceptual quality than min ADE/FDE.
Contribution of a unified benchmark with textual descriptions and a commitment to release data and code, which could benefit follow-up work.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The core method is a direct combination of standard DDPM (continuous) and multinomial diffusion (discrete) under a shared denoiser, essentially U2Diff's architecture plus a classification head. Joint continuous-discrete diffusion already exists for layout generation, CAD sketches, and vision-language modeling (Levi et al., 2023; Chereddy & Femiani, 2025; Li et al., 2025); applying it to sports trajectories is an application-level, incremental extension, not a new modeling principle.

The 'discrete events' are largely redundant with the continuous data: possession events E are extracted from the trajectories Y via a simple 1.5-meter heuristic (Appendix C.1), and the guidance signals G_WPG/G_text are derived from those same heuristic events. This substantially weakens the central claim that joint modeling captures meaningful extra structure — the discrete modality is almost a deterministic function of the trajectories. The paper does not analyze how much independent information E actually provides (e.g., no experiment with genuinely annotated event data for at least one dataset).

The controllability story is confusing and possibly overstated. The paper describes CFG training (25% condition dropout) but then states that at inference 'we can achieve effective guidance by using a single forward pass with the conditional output' — i.e., no actual classifier-free guidance scale is used. This makes the heavy CFG framing misleading and raises questions about whether the conditioning mechanism behaves as claimed.

Improvements over the strongest baseline (U2Diff) are consistent but modest (e.g., SADE 2.59->2.36 on NFL), and the gains of the joint model over 'Ours w/o joint' in Table 2 are small and not accompanied by statistical significance tests or error bars across seeds.

The human evaluation is thin: 15 participants, only NBA, n=35-50 pairwise comparisons per baseline, and models are selected by minimum SADE before judging, which conflates metric selection with human preference.

Incomplete baselines: LED could not be trained on NFL/BundesLiga due to GPU memory, and the comparison between IID and non-IID models on min vs. avg metrics makes some table entries hard to interpret as true SOTA claims.

Clarity and polish issues: grammatical errors remain (e.g., Figure 1/13 captions 'Player 1 is starts with the ball'), the 'is possessed' typo in Sec. 4.1, and the S^d / S^c notation in the Beta Schedule paragraph is used inconsistently (S/Sc vs. S/S^d), which makes the schedule hard to follow.
The imputation comparison in Table 1-bottom and Table 4 mixes metrics (BADE vs. SADE) and masking protocols that differ from prior work, complicating direct comparability despite the claimed SOTA.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper is (to the authors' justified knowledge) the first to apply joint continuous-discrete diffusion to time-evolving multi-agent systems, and the formulation (factorized forward processes, factorized reverse via a shared denoiser conditioned on the full state, decomposed variational bound) is sound and clearly presented.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three public sports datasets (NBA, NFL, BundesLiga), multiple strong baselines (GroupNet, AutoBots, LED, MART, MoFlow, Sports-Traj, U2Diff, TranSPORTmer) retrained with documented settings, and consistent SOTA results on scene-level metrics for both future and imputation generation.

Goes beyond non-controllable generation with two new controllable tasks (weak-possessor-guidance and text-guidance), supported by the CrossGuid conditioning module and a curated text-annotated benchmark, which is a useful resource for the community.

Good ablation coverage: discrete denoising steps, DDIM skip interval, joint-loss weight lambda, importance sampling, number of Social Transformer layers, and an attention-entropy interpretability analysis supporting the joint-modeling hypothesis.
Human evaluation with 15 participants corroborates that avg (scene-level) metrics better reflect perceptual quality than min ADE/FDE, an interesting observation for the evaluation-protocol debate.
Limitations are honestly discussed (dense-event assumption, heuristic event extraction for NFL), and the authors commit to releasing data and code, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the core technique is a fairly direct combination of established components (DDPM + multinomial diffusion (Hoogeboom et al.) + CFG + DDIM hybrid sampling + a beta-schedule alignment trick from DLT). The main claim of 'first joint continuous-discrete diffusion for spatio-temporal systems' is a domain-level first rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

Ground-truth possession events E are derived from trajectories via a simple 1.5 m proximity heuristic, so the discrete labels the model is trained and evaluated on are themselves noisy and partially circular; the impact of label noise on the claimed benefits of joint modeling is not analyzed (e.g., comparison against genuinely annotated event data, which exists for BundesLiga).

Controllable-generation evaluation conditions on ground-truth guidance signals extracted from the test scenes; there is no evaluation on held-out or human-written prompts, and no external baseline for the controllable tasks (the only comparison is the authors' own w/o-joint variant), making it hard to judge the absolute strength of the controllability results.

The human study is small (15 participants, 128 scenes, one dataset) and the min-SADE mode-selection protocol for the study may favor the best-case behavior; the claimed 'metrics do not correlate with human judgment' conclusion rests on thin evidence.

Some claims are under-specified: e.g., the statement that effective CFG guidance is achieved 'using a single forward pass with the conditional output' is not clearly explained (how this differs from standard CFG, and why it works), and the guidance scale / mechanism is not ablated.

Text-guidance is missing for NBA, and the BundesLiga dataset is small (7 matches, ~2k scenes after augmentation), so generality of the text-guidance conclusions is limited; failure cases confirm the model struggles with text conditioning.

A few presentation issues: notation errors in Eq. 6 (mu_theta defined with inconsistent arguments), occasional grammar problems (e.g., 'Player 1 is starts', 'predict' should be 'predicts'), and the 'C' constant in Eq. 1 is loosely described.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: jointly modeling continuous trajectories and discrete possession events in multi-agent dynamic systems is a genuine gap, and the paper is, to my knowledge, the first to apply joint continuous-discrete diffusion to temporally evolving multi-agent domains rather than static tasks.

The methodological composition is sound: multinomial diffusion for discrete events combined with Gaussian diffusion for trajectories, with a clean derivation of the factorized variational bound, a hybrid DDIM/multinomial sampler, and a thoughtful beta-schedule alignment between discrete and continuous denoising steps.

Comprehensive evaluation: three sports datasets (NBA, NFL, newly curated Bundesliga with text descriptions), comparisons against many recent baselines (GroupNet, LED, MART, MoFlow, U2Diff, Sports-Traj, TranSPORTmer), scene-level metrics (SADE/SFDE), a human perceptual study, consistency analysis between predicted events and trajectories, and extensive ablations (discrete steps, loss weighting λ, guidance strength, T5 encoder size, multinomial vs. absorbing state, importance sampling, attention entropy interpretability).

The controllability contributions (weak-possessor-guidance and text-guidance via CrossGuid) are novel tasks for dynamic multi-agent domains, and the results consistently show that joint modeling improves both trajectory quality and control accuracy over a non-joint ablation.
Release of a unified text-enhanced benchmark (code/dataloaders promised) adds community value; limitations and failure cases are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited: the framework is a relatively straightforward composition of DDPM + multinomial diffusion (both established), with an architecture inherited from U2Diff (Capellera et al., 2025). CrossGuid is essentially standard cross-attention with modality-specific design choices. The main novelty is the application setting and the controllable tasks rather than new modeling principles.

The discrete 'events' are not independent supervision: possessor labels are extracted from the trajectory data itself via a 1.5m distance heuristic (Appendix C.1). This makes the 'joint modeling' somewhat circular—the discrete modality is a deterministic-ish function of the continuous one—raising the question of whether joint diffusion genuinely captures coupled discrete dynamics or merely a redundant re-encoding, and how well this transfers to genuinely independent event streams.

Some gains over the closest baseline (U2Diff) are modest and improvement over the non-joint ablation, while consistent, is not dramatic; error bars/confidence intervals and statistical significance tests are absent, so claims of SOTA rest on single-run numbers.

Human evaluation is small-scale (15 participants, ~50 comparisons per pairing) and the min-metric selection for display favors models with better best-of-20 modes; the human vs. ADE/FDE discrepancy argument would benefit from more rigorous study.

Evaluation of the absorbing-state comparison relies on a hyperparameter (absorption rate λ=0.01) tuned only to match loss magnitudes; a fairer tuning protocol would strengthen the claim that multinomial is superior in dynamic domains.

Several key details (e.g., how text descriptions correlate with guidance accuracy, sensitivity to heuristic threshold errors, dataset quality control for LLM-generated captions) are deferred to the appendix, and dataset/code release is only promised upon acceptance, limiting immediate reproducibility.

strengths: The problem setting—jointly generating continuous multi-agent trajectories and synchronous discrete events—is well motivated, and the paper is the first to bring joint continuous-discrete diffusion to a temporally evolving dynamic domain rather than static tasks like layout generation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three datasets (NBA, NFL, Bundesliga), including completion (future and imputation) with appropriate scene-level metrics (SADE/SFDE), a controllable generation study (WPG and text-guidance), a multinomial-vs-absorbing-state consistency analysis, and extensive ablations (denoising steps, loss weighting lambda, guidance strength, T5 encoder size, importance sampling, social transformer count).
Inclusion of a human preference study, which is rare in this literature, and a thoughtful argument that avg/scene-level metrics correlate better with perceptual quality than min ADE/FDE.

Clear exposition of the method (factorized forward processes, factorized variational bound, hybrid DDIM/multinomial sampling with aligned discrete schedule), a new annotated text-guidance benchmark, and a stated commitment to releasing code and data.
Failure cases and limitations are discussed openly, and LLM usage and ethics statements are provided.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution is a fairly direct composition of two well-known diffusion processes (DDPM Gaussian diffusion + multinomial diffusion from Hoogeboom et al. 2021) with a factorized joint bound; the derivations follow straightforwardly from existing work, and CrossGuid is a standard cross-attention residual injection plus classifier-free guidance. The 'first joint continuous-discrete diffusion for dynamic domains' claim is the main novelty argument, which is a positioning claim rather than a methodological advance.

A circularity concern in the evaluation: the discrete possession events E are extracted from the trajectories Y themselves via a 1.5m proximity heuristic, and the consistency metric compares predicted events against the heuristic possessor recomputed from predicted trajectories. Since the event supervision is a deterministic function of the trajectories, high consistency may partly reflect the model learning the heuristic mapping rather than genuine semantic coupling; a comparison with independent (e.g., annotated) event streams is missing for NBA, and NFL event labels themselves are assigned by heuristic.

Controllable generation is evaluated only by conditioning on ground-truth guidance signals and against the paper's own non-joint ablation ('Ours w/o joint'); there is no external baseline or alternative conditioning method for controllability (e.g., other guidance techniques), making it hard to judge whether CrossGuid and the joint framework are actually the best way to achieve this control.

The advantage of joint modeling is modest in places: Table 2 shows small gains of the joint model over the non-joint variant on trajectory metrics, and the human-evaluation win rate over 'w/o joint' is only 53% (67% excluding ties), which weakens the central claim that joint modeling is 'crucial'.

Scope is narrow: the framework requires discrete events to share the exact spatio-temporal grid of the trajectories (acknowledged limitation), confining applicability to dense, grid-aligned event streams like sports possession; claims of relevance to autonomous driving and robotics are not substantiated by any experiment in those domains.

Some evaluation details raise fairness questions: several baselines (LED on NFL/Bundesliga, NBA text-guidance) could not be run, baselines were retrained by the authors with adapted hyperparameters, and the human study is small (15 participants, 15 pairs).

The new Bundesliga dataset (7 matches, 2k scenes) is small, and the authors themselves attribute failure cases to this; its value as a community benchmark versus existing alternatives (e.g., Soccer-U) is asserted rather than established.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: jointly modeling continuous trajectories and synchronous discrete events in multi-agent systems is a genuine gap, and the sports domain is a natural testbed.

Technically sound formulation: the joint forward/reverse diffusion with factorized transitions, decomposed variational bound (Eq. 8), and hybrid sampling (DDIM for continuous, multinomial posterior for discrete, with an aligned hybrid beta schedule) is carefully derived and internally consistent.

Comprehensive evaluation: three public datasets (NBA, NFL, Bundesliga), two completion tasks (future and imputation), controllable generation with two novel conditioning modalities (WPG and text), a consistency analysis comparing multinomial vs. absorbing diffusion, and an ablation suite (denoising steps, lambda, guidance weight, T5 encoder size, importance sampling, ST layers).

Human evaluation (15 participants, pairwise comparisons) adds credibility to perceptual-quality claims and is used to argue that scene-level SADE/SFDE metrics correlate better with human preference than min ADE/FDE.
Honest failure analysis and limitations section (sparse event processes not supported, NFL actor labeling relies on heuristics, dataset size constraints for text-guidance).
Contribution of a unified benchmark with textual descriptions and a commitment to release code/data supports reproducibility and future work.
weaknesses: Core novelty is incremental: the method is essentially a composition of known components (DDPM for continuous modality, multinomial diffusion from Hoogeboom et al. 2021 for discrete modality, classifier-free guidance, and cross-attention conditioning in CrossGuid). The 'first joint continuous-discrete diffusion for dynamic multi-agent systems' claim is plausible but the architectural and algorithmic novelty beyond prior joint diffusion work (Levi et al. 2023; Li et al. 2025; Chereddy & Femiani 2025) is modest.

Absolute gains over the strongest baseline (U2Diff) are small (e.g., NFL SADE 2.36 vs 2.59, imputation 0.84 vs 0.96), and no statistical significance or variance across seeds is reported; given training-set sizes, this leaves some uncertainty about robustness.

Guidance signals (GWPG, Gtext) are derived from ground-truth/heuristic possessor labels rather than independent annotations; the 1.5m possession heuristic, though empirically justified, could inject systematic label noise, and text descriptions are LLM-generated from the same trajectory features the model sees, which may inflate controllability accuracy.
The human study is small (15 participants, 15 pairs per comparison, single dataset), so conclusions about perceptual superiority and metric correlation should be treated as preliminary.

Several baselines could not be fully trained on NFL/Bundesliga (LED dropped for memory; TranSPORTmer missing SFDE), and much of the baseline infrastructure comes from the same research group (U2Diff, TranSPORTmer), which weakens independent comparability.
Text-guidance is unavailable on NBA, so the headline text-guidance results rest on the two smaller datasets only.
Reproducibility relies on promised releases; dataset construction (LLM-refined captions, heuristic event extraction) involves non-trivial choices not fully verifiable from the paper.
